name: JBF theory (just be first)

lead: JBF ("just be first") is a looksmaxxing-community theory holding that the person who first gets close to someone romantically, often early in life, tends to win the relationship regardless of looks. It is raised alongside discussion of why less conventionally attractive men sometimes have partners.

The appearance angle is indirect: proponents use it to argue that approaching early and often, not only facial or physical traits, shapes dating outcomes. No studies have tested the theory under that name, though research on first impressions, proximity and mere exposure covers related ideas.

paras: In practice it is a way of interpreting dating outcomes and a motivation to initiate contact early. Forum users share anecdotes of first partners, couples who met young, and celebrity relationships that began before fame.
There are no physical risks. Community members dispute it; some replies on looksmax.org argue that attractiveness still matters more than timing.

chain: Higher chance of a relationship, per proponents
angle.text: Proponents use JBF to argue that initiating contact early improves dating outcomes alongside, or in place of, physical appearance. It is a framework for behaviour and timing rather than a change to how someone looks.

lead: JBF theory, short for "just be first", is a belief discussed on looksmaxxing forums that the person who is first to date or reach a partner "wins" them, with timing and initiative mattering more than relative attractiveness.[1] It is usually offered as an explanation for couples in which one partner appears more conventionally attractive than the other.[2]

Threads on looksmax.org cite examples such as models who dated before their careers began, and users describe their own early relationships as evidence.[2] Others in the same threads push back, arguing that good bone structure and height are what actually decide outcomes.[2]

No published trial is known to test JBF theory by name. Adjacent research includes the mere-exposure effect, in which people tend to like things and people they encounter repeatedly, described by Zajonc in 1968,[3] and the propinquity effect in attraction research.[4]
infobox: Whoever approaches or bonds first tends to win the match [1]

paras: The theory states that being first to date or become close to someone gives a decisive advantage in forming a relationship.[1] One forum poster asks whether it also applies to men, describing a middle-school relationship that he and his ex-partner both keep returning to.[1] Proponents frame it as a counterweight to purely looks-based explanations of dating, while critics frame it as a partial explanation at most.[2]

Several looksmax.org threads are titled around the idea, some calling it highly accurate, others discussing a 'just be first pill', and others posting a vlog and a thread on its significance.[5][6][7][8][9] A thread on a model couple who met when both were new to modeling, and who dated for years before going public, uses their history as an example; a reply counters that 'its not just be first, its dont be ugly'.[2] Another thread applies the label to a pop singer's ex-boyfriend.[10]
The term sits within a family of dating-theory vocabulary on the forum, where users discuss whether timing, familiarity, looks, height or social status best explain who ends up with whom.

The mere-exposure effect, popularised by Robert Zajonc's 1968 paper, is the tendency to like things more as they become familiar; in attraction research, people tend to like someone more the more often they see them.[3] Bornstein's 1989 meta-analysis of 208 experiments found the effect reliable (r = 0.26), strongest for unfamiliar stimuli, typically peaking within 10 to 20 exposures and, in some analyses, declining afterwards.[3]

A 1992 study by Moreland and Beach had four similar-looking women attend a college class for 0, 5, 10 or 15 sessions, finding that familiarity mediated the link between exposure and attraction.[4] Researchers also describe a 'social allergy effect' in which repeated exposure can produce annoyance with a partner's behaviours.[4]

Attraction research also covers physical attractiveness and the matching hypothesis, the idea that lasting couples tend to be similar in attractiveness; studies by Walster and colleagues (1971) and Murstein and Christy (1976) are cited in support.[4] These literatures address familiarity and looks separately and do not test the 'first' framing.
No studies found. Related laboratory and social-psychology research on familiarity and attraction is summarised in the Related research section.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the theory is both promoted as a counterweight to looks-only views and disputed by those who prioritise appearance.[2]
